report.sop_markdown:
**Rahul Sharma | Applicant, MSc, Department of Computer Science, University of Toronto | 2026–2027**

The first time I watched a retrieval-augmented chatbot answer a question from 4,000 pages of course notes in 1.2 seconds, I was less interested in the demo than in the 4.8 seconds I had removed. That project began with a simple problem: my peers and I had too many notes and too little time. I built a retrieval pipeline using sentence-transformer embeddings and FAISS, served it through FastAPI, and added caching that cut answer latency from six seconds to 1.2 seconds. The lesson stayed with me: a language-model system is only useful when retrieval, latency, and evaluation are treated as first-class engineering problems.

I am a final-year B.Tech Computer Science and Engineering student at Lovely Professional University, expected to graduate in 2027 with a CGPA of 8.2/10. My coursework and project work have given me experience across Python, PyTorch, FastAPI, SQL, Docker, Git, and LangChain, as well as retrieval-augmented generation, LLM training and pretraining, transformer architectures, BPE tokenization, finetuning and evaluation, CUDA/C/C++, React and JavaScript, OpenRouter-based multi-LLM orchestration, Jupyter Notebook, shell scripting, optimizers such as AdamW and Muon, mixed-precision training, and technical course development. I also have half a year of work experience, which has made me more disciplined about shipping maintainable code rather than one-off notebooks. At Lovely Professional University I served as a teaching assistant for the Python programming lab, and I was a runner-up at Smart India Hackathon 2025 with a team of four. Both experiences reinforced something I value in research: clear explanations and reproducible work matter as much as the final result.

My projects sit at the intersection of applied machine learning and practical systems. The RAG Chatbot for Course Notes required me to chunk and embed a large corpus, tune retrieval, and keep the API responsive; the latency work was as important as the model choice. The Resume Parser was a different kind of evaluation problem. I fine-tuned a small transformer to extract education, skills, and experience from resumes and measured 91% field-level accuracy on a 500-document test set. That project taught me to define error categories, inspect failures, and treat evaluation as an ongoing part of model development rather than a final checkbox. Together, these projects have prepared me for research that combines model behavior with the engineering needed to test it at scale.

The University of Toronto Department of Computer Science is a strong fit because its research-stream graduate program is built around exactly that combination. The Department offers a funding package to all full-time research-stream students, composed of a research assistantship and teaching assistantships, with an enhanced package that ensures a take-home living allowance of $39,500 after tuition and incidentals are paid, plus up to $17,250 CAD for students admitted in 2026–2027. Funding is guaranteed for a defined period, conditional on satisfactory progress, and is 16 months for the MSc. That structure matters to me: the research assistantship would let me commit deeply to a lab, while the teaching assistantship connects to the work I have already done in the Python programming lab. I am applying to the research-stream MSc in Computer Science, and I would like to work with [ADD: U of T faculty member/lab and one representative paper]. I also understand that all graduate students are required to apply for and accept external awards for which they are eligible, and that students in good academic standing must apply for the Departmental Fellowship by reporting external scholarships, stipends, and paid employment to the Graduate Office. I will meet those requirements.

After the degree, I want to work as a research engineer or research scientist on language-model systems, with a focus on retrieval, evaluation, and efficient training. I am particularly interested in making LLM pipelines more reliable and more transparent, so that gains in model quality are matched by gains in testability. The Department’s research areas in computer science and artificial intelligence, together with its research assistantship and teaching assistantship model, would give me the environment to pursue that goal seriously.

I would be grateful for the opportunity to contribute to the Department of Computer Science at the University of Toronto.
